Bellini announced it one November evening, at the trattoria, at the end of dinner, tapping his glass with a teaspoon as people do at weddings. "I'm sixty-three," he said, "with a heart repaired with a stent and a published book. The time has come to really retire. Not just for show, like two years ago." There was silence. Then Graziella said she didn't believe it, because he had said the same thing at least three times. Bellini smiled. "This time it's true," he replied. "And to prove it, I'm leaving you the workshop. Not just the key. Everything. The walls, the brushes, the debts. Above all the debts."

The workshop, in fact, had never belonged to Giulia and Matei. It had remained Bellini's, who had inherited it from his father, who in turn had inherited it from Ernesto. Giulia, Matei and Chiara worked there and ran it, but he was the owner. Now Bellini wanted to change things. His idea was simple and a little crazy: to turn the workshop into a cooperative, in which Giulia, Matei and Chiara would be equal partners. He would hand over everything for a symbolic euro, "because things given as gifts are not respected, and things paid for too dearly are regretted".

There was, however, a problem. To set up the cooperative and buy the new machine for analyses, the one Giulia had used in Malta and which no private workshop in Florence had, money was needed. About thirty thousand euros. And to get a bank loan, you had to present a balance sheet and a business plan. Giulia knew how to restore a Caravaggio, Matei could recognise an eighteenth-century fake from ten metres away, Chiara could embroider silk with a fever. But none of the three had ever read a balance sheet in their lives.

So they called Valeria. The neighbourhood councillor arrived one Sunday afternoon with a laptop, a pocket calculator and a stack of sheets that Bellini had taken out of a cupboard, handwritten over forty years of black notebooks. "But this isn't a balance sheet," said Valeria, leafing through them. "It's a diary." Bellini nodded, not at all embarrassed. "My grandfather noted income and expenses next to the restorations," he explained. "I carried on. 14 March 1987: income, a hundred lire for a retouch. Expense, two sandwiches." Valeria put her head in her hands. Then she laughed. "All right," she said. "It'll take a week. But it can be done."

Graziella, passing with the coffee, looked at the black notebooks on the table and shook her head. "Amateurs," she said. Then she went into the kitchen and came back with a squared notebook, stained with oil, its cover held together with sticky tape. "This is the trattoria's balance sheet since 1974," she said. "Every evening, before going to bed, I write down how much I took and how much I spent. My father did the same, and my grandmother before him." Valeria leafed through it, incredulous. The pages were full of neat figures, perfect columns, totals underlined in red. "Madam," she said, "this is more accurate than a bank's." Graziella shrugged. "In the kitchen, if you get the sums wrong, the ribollita isn't enough for everyone," she replied. "Banks, on the other hand, when they get it wrong, ask for a loan."

In fact, it took ten days. Valeria stopped by the workshop every evening after the council meetings and, together with Chiara, who turned out to be surprisingly good with figures, turned Bellini's black notebooks into tables. Matei made the coffee. Giulia looked for invoices in the drawers. Davide, who was now fourteen and came to the workshop every afternoon, drew the charts by hand, with coloured pencils, because he said computer charts were "as ugly as statistics". And Pietro, who had started at the liceo classico in September, checked that the percentages were written correctly in Italian.

The figures, in the end, told a story nobody expected. The year's income had been about one hundred and twenty thousand euros, compared with one hundred thousand the year before: an increase of twenty per cent, almost all thanks to the restoration in Malta and the fame that came after the story of the T. Expenses had risen too, but less: spending on materials had almost doubled, because old pigments cost more and more, but the rent had fallen by a third thanks to the Shops Project. The final profit was just under ten thousand euros. "You're not rich," said Valeria. "But you're alive. And a living workshop, in the Oltrarno, is already a miracle."

The business plan was the hardest part. You had to explain to the bank why, with a new machine for analyses, the workshop would earn more. Valeria did some research: in Tuscany there were about a hundred small churches and museums that every year had to analyse their works before a restoration, and almost all of them sent the samples to Rome or Milan, waiting for months. "If you do it here, in a week," she said, "you could have about twenty new clients a year. Turnover would rise by about thirty per cent. In three years the loan would be paid back." Matei looked at her with admiration. "You should be minister of the economy," he said. "Heaven forbid," replied Valeria. "The neighbourhood is enough for me."

To be sure of the calculation, they called Karl, the apprentice from Malta, who was now studying art history in Rome with Professor Ruggeri and knew the machine well. Karl answered by video call from the university library, whispering. He explained that the machine made it possible to analyse a pigment in an hour instead of three weeks, and that in Malta, during the six months of the restoration, they had used it more than two hundred times. "The cost of each analysis is about ten euros," he said. "At an outside laboratory, it costs over a hundred." Chiara did the sum on the calculator and was left open-mouthed. "Ninety euros saved each time," she said. "Multiplied by two hundred…" "Eighteen thousand euros," said Davide, before her, without a calculator. Everyone looked at him. "I've been doing sums for paints since I was ten," he explained.

The meeting at the bank was set for a Tuesday morning in December, at a branch in via dei Serragli. Giulia, Matei and Chiara turned up dressed as if for a wedding, with a folder full of tables and Davide's coloured charts. The branch manager, Dr Gori, was a man of fifty with thin glasses and a grey tie, who received them with the cold politeness of someone who has seen hundreds of business plans and approved very few. He leafed through the balance sheet in silence, then stopped at the charts. "Who made these?" he asked. "A fourteen-year-old boy," replied Chiara. "Our apprentice."

Dr Gori raised an eyebrow. Then he asked a series of precise questions, one after another, like a doctor examining a patient. How many loyal clients did they have? About ten. What percentage of income came from abroad? Just under forty per cent, thanks to Malta. What would happen if the Malta restoration were not repeated? Income would fall by about a third. At this question Giulia hesitated. It was the weak point of the plan, and everyone knew it. The manager noted something in his notebook. "I see," he said. It was an "I see" that promised nothing good.

At that very moment Giulia's phone vibrated in her bag. She ignored it, embarrassed. It vibrated again. And then a third time. Dr Gori, with a wave of his hand, told her to answer. It was Camilleri, from Malta. Giulia listened for a minute, without saying anything, her eyes widening. Then she covered the phone with her hand and turned to Matei and Chiara. "The Co-Cathedral," she said quietly. "They want to entrust us with the restoration of two more paintings. Mattia Preti. Next year. A three-year contract." Chiara put a hand to her mouth. Matei looked at the bank manager, who had heard everything.

Dr Gori took off his glasses, wiped them calmly and, for the first time in the whole meeting, smiled. "A three-year contract abroad," he said, "reduces the risk by about half. Compared with the plan you presented to me, your turnover could rise not by thirty, but by fifty per cent." He took a pen. "I propose thirty thousand euros, over five years, at an interest rate of three point five per cent. But on one condition." The three of them stiffened. "I want to meet the boy who made the charts," said the manager. "In twenty years at the bank, I have never seen a balance sheet drawn so beautifully."

Davide went to the bank the next day, accompanied by his mother, Rita, in an ironed shirt and with his hair combed with water. Dr Gori showed him his charts, pinned to the noticeboard in his office, and asked him why he had drawn them by hand. Davide thought for a moment. "Because the figures on the computer are all the same," he replied. "But these figures are different. This one here is the Caravaggio in Malta. This is the angel from Prato. This is the banner from San Frediano. Every figure is a painting. You can't draw it like a statistic." The manager looked at him for a long time. Then he asked Rita whether her son had already thought about what he wanted to be when he grew up.

"A restorer," replied Davide, before his mother could open her mouth. Dr Gori nodded slowly. "Pity," he said. "I would have liked to offer you an internship at the bank, when you're eighteen. But it seems the paintings have already won." He shook his hand as you do with an adult. Leaving the bank, Rita told Davide that it was the first time anyone had offered her a job, and he was fourteen. Davide replied that it wasn't a job. It was a compliment. And that compliments, as he had learned at the workshop, are worth more than money, but less than ribollita.

The cooperative was founded on 20 December, before a notary, in the office in via Maggio that had once belonged to the old notary Bardi, the lawyer's father. There were three partners: Giulia Esposito, Matei Popa and Chiara Benedetti, each with a third of the shares. The name was chosen by Bellini, and nobody had the courage to argue with it: "Cooperativa di restauro Ernesto". No surname. "Because Ernesto was the name of a man who worked with his hands," he explained. "The surname was just the signature. And signatures, as we now know, sometimes hide a T."

That evening Matei phoned Sibiu to give his parents the news. Ion listened to everything in silence, as he always did, then asked a single question: "How much?" Matei explained the loan, the interest, the years, the shares. Ion was silent for a long time. Matei thought he was worried. Then he heard a rustle of paper at the other end of the phone. "I've done the sum," said Ion. "At three point five per cent over five years, you'll pay about two thousand seven hundred euros in interest. That's less than I've spent coming to Florence by train over these years." He paused. "All right. Do it. And if you don't make it, I'll sell the watch." Matei laughed. He knew his father would never sell the watch. But he also knew that, for the first time, he had offered it.

Bellini handed over the workshop for one euro, as he had promised. He took it out of his wallet in front of the notary: a one-euro coin, new and shiny, with Leonardo's Vitruvian Man on it. He gave it to Giulia, who gave it to the notary, who put it on the table next to the contract. Then Bellini signed. He signed with Ernesto's tiny brush, dipped in ink, as he had signed Valeria's candidacy. The notary protested that it wasn't regular. Bellini replied that, in forty years of restorations, the most regular thing he had ever seen was a brush in the hand of someone who knows how to use it.

That evening, at the trattoria, there was a small party. Graziella made ribollita, of course, and a new dessert, an apple pie she had learned from Doina, with "Coop. Ernesto" written on it in icing sugar. Bellini made a short toast. "When I took over this workshop from my father," he said, "it brought in about ten thousand euros a year, in today's money. Today it brings in one hundred and twenty thousand. In forty years turnover has grown twelvefold. But that isn't what I'm proudest of." He paused. "It's that, when I took it over, I worked there alone. Today three partners work there, an apprentice, a Saturday consultant and a boy who writes the diary. That's the only figure that counts."

"A Saturday consultant?" asked Chiara. "Who is it?" Bellini pointed at Valeria, who blushed. "Her," he said. "From today, every Saturday morning, Councillor Conti will come to the workshop to check the accounts. For free. She promised this evening, at the second glass of wine." Valeria protested that she didn't remember promising. Graziella, from the kitchen, said she had heard her very well and that in the Oltrarno promises made at the second glass are worth more than those made before a notary. Everyone laughed. And Valeria, in the end, raised her glass. "All right," she said. "But I'm not drinking the third glass. Otherwise I'll end up doing your tax returns too."

Later, after the guests had left, Pietro opened the black notebook and wrote the date: 20 December. Below, he tried to sum up the day in figures, as he had learned in those weeks. "Partners: three. Shares: a third each. Price of the workshop: one euro. Loan: thirty thousand euros, at three point five per cent. Expected increase in turnover: about fifty per cent. Turnover multiplied by twelve in forty years." Then he stopped, reread it and added a line below: "Number of ribollitas served this evening: about sixty. Number of happy people: all of them. Percentage: one hundred per cent."

Davide, who had slept at the trattoria because his mother was on the night shift, read the page over Pietro's shoulder and shook his head. "Something's missing," he said. He took the coloured pencils and, at the bottom of the page, drew a very small chart: a line rising from the bottom, with dates written beneath. 1904, Ernesto is born. 1966, the mud. 1974, Aldo and the ribollita. Malta. The cooperative. The line rose, sometimes fell, but in the end it reached the top, beyond the edge of the page. Above it, Davide wrote the title: "The turnover of happiness". Pietro looked at him and laughed. "That," he said, "no bank would understand." "Exactly," replied Davide. "That's why it goes in the diary."
